8.title: the hands nobody sees
8.hook: the shoes handed back, the plates scrubbed, the roti rolled by someone you'll never meet; the word for that
8.tomorrow: the first symbol of the scripture
8.howItsDone: Sikhs do seva in the gurdwara by cooking and serving langar, cleaning, washing dishes and looking after shoes, and outside it through relief work and community service, usually as unpaid volunteers.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the Khanda: the inner and the outer, held together. Week two starts with the hands. Day eight.

You leave your shoes at the gurdwara door, and when you come back they're lined up waiting, sometimes wiped clean. Someone scrubbed the plate you ate langar from. Someone rolled the roti. In the great kitchen in Amritsar, a banker chops onions beside a teenager washing steel plates. Nobody's keeping score, and nobody asks your name. There's a word for what those hands are doing.
screen: `YOUR SHOES, HANDED BACK.` → `A BANKER CHOPPING ONIONS.` → `NOBODY KEEPING SCORE.`

segments.voice: The word is seva: selfless service, done for others with no reward in mind. Here's what makes it different from just being nice. In Sikh life it's part of the spiritual life, not something beside it. The Gurus return to the idea again and again: service done with a humble heart is a way of drawing near to God. Not a warm-up for the real practice. The practice. Hands in the dishwater count. And seva has a condition: it's meant to be done without ego. The hymns warn that service done to be seen, thanked or admired quietly turns into something else. That's why so much of it happens where nobody's watching. The person who scrubbed your plate doesn't know your name, and that isn't an accident. Sikh teaching names three kinds: with your body, like cooking or cleaning; with your mind, like teaching or listening; and with what you have, like food or money. So there's no one who can't do it. And if you've seen Sikh volunteers turn up with hot meals after a flood or a fire, now you know the word they'd use.
screen: `SEVA — SELFLESS SERVICE.` · `NOT BESIDE THE PRACTICE. THE PRACTICE.` · `DONE WITHOUT EGO.` · `BODY, MIND, AND WHAT YOU HAVE.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and bring to mind one person who could use a hand. Not a grand gesture: a dish, a message, a door held. Picture yourself doing it without telling anyone. Stay with that picture for a while: one person, one quiet thing.
Seva. Selfless service, done without ego, and part of the spiritual life itself. Eighth word.
Your line: one quiet thing for someone. Seva works best when nobody hears about it, not even over dinner. Day eight.

screen: `DAY 8 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE FIRST SYMBOL OF THE SCRIPTURE.`

9.title: the first symbol of the scripture
9.hook: the first symbol of the scripture — one
9.howItsDone: Ik Onkar opens the Guru Granth Sahib and begins the Mool Mantar, which Sikhs recite daily; the symbol is written, painted and worn as a reminder of the one God.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seva. Your line was one quiet thing for someone. Today, the very first mark in the Sikh scripture. Day nine.

Most books start with a title, or once upon a time. The Sikh scripture, the Guru Granth Sahib, starts with a symbol. You may have seen it without knowing: on a gold pendant, a dashboard, over a shop door, on a forearm. A Gurmukhi numeral with a sweeping curve flying off the top. Before any story, any rule, any song: this.
screen: `A LONG BOOK OF HYMNS.` → `THE FIRST THING ISN'T A WORD.` → `IT'S A SYMBOL.`

segments.voice: It's called Ik Onkar. It starts with a numeral: the digit one. Not the word, the number, the one you'd write on a price tag. That's Ik. Then Onkar, a very old sound for the divine, related to Om, which Nanak's Hindu neighbors chanted. And the curve, sweeping up and out, which some Sikhs read as a line with no end. Together: there is one. One God, one reality, one source behind everything. Why a numeral? One way Sikh teachers explain it: a word belongs to one language, and can be argued with. Everyone agrees on one. And notice what that one includes. On this path, the one isn't far off, looking down on creation. The hymns say it's in everything: in you, in the person across the street, in the river and the dust. So if there's one, nobody stands outside it. You can hear Guru Nanak's line from day six underneath: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. If there's one, the labels come second.
screen: `IK — THE NUMERAL ONE.` · `ONKAR — AN ANCIENT SOUND FOR GOD.` · `A NUMBER NOBODY CAN ARGUE WITH.` · `IF THERE'S ONE, NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and notice yourself: your hands, your chest rising. Then notice something beyond you: a sound in the room, someone you love. Then hold both at once, and if you like, let one word ride out on the breath: one.
Ik Onkar. The numeral one, joined to an ancient sound for God: there is one, and it opens the whole scripture. Ninth word.
Your line: one. Same source, for you and for the person who annoys you most. That's day nine.

screen: `DAY 9 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: "ONE CREATOR, TRUTH IS THE NAME."`

10.title: "one creator, truth is the name"
10.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the Mool Mantar at the start of the morning prayer Japji Sahib and at many other times; it stands at the head of the Guru Granth Sahib and is often the first passage children memorize.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ik Onkar, the numeral one that opens the scripture. Today, the words that come right after it. Day ten.

Describe God in a single breath. Not a book, not a sermon: a few words, short enough for a child to memorize and deep enough for a lifetime. Right after the symbol for one, at the top of the scripture, Guru Nanak does exactly that. Sikhs call it the Mool Mantar, the root verse, and many say it every morning. Today, its first line.
screen: `DESCRIBE GOD IN ONE BREATH.` → `THE ROOT VERSE.` → `A SEED THAT HOLDS A TREE.`

segments.voice: Mool means root. Mantar is the Punjabi form of mantra, a sacred phrase. The scripture's language is centuries old, and even fluent Punjabi speakers look words up, so one line at a time is how everyone reads it. After Ik Onkar, it says: Sat Naam. Karta Purakh. Sat means truth, and something deeper than true as opposed to false: it comes from an old root meaning what really is, what lasts. Naam means name. Sat Naam: truth is the name, or the one whose name is truth. The Victorian scholar Max Arthur Macauliffe, who translated with Sikh scholars beside him, gave the opening as: "There is but one God whose name is true, the Creator." Here's the surprise in naam. On this path the name isn't just a label, like yours printed on a bill. It comes to mean the whole presence of God, running through everything. Then Karta Purakh. Karta, the maker. Purakh, the being. The creator: not a force that set the world going and walked away, but the one still making. Three ideas in five words: there is one, its name is truth, and it creates. And a quiet challenge inside: if truth is God's name, then telling the truth is a way of saying it.
screen: `MOOL MANTAR — THE ROOT VERSE.` · `SAT — WHAT REALLY IS.` · `NAAM — MORE THAN A LABEL.` · `KARTA PURAKH — THE ONE STILL MAKING.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and think of one true thing about your life right now: not the flattering version, just the true one. Sit with it without fixing it. If you like, let two words go out with the breath: Sat Naam.
The Mool Mantar, the root verse. Line one: Ik Onkar, Sat Naam, Karta Purakh. There is one, truth is the name, the creator. Tenth word.
Your line: the name is truth. Which makes an honest sentence a small way of saying it. Day ten.

11.title: "without fear, without hate"
11.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the whole Mool Mantar, including nirbhau and nirvair, at the start of Japji Sahib each morning, and the phrase is often held up as an ideal for how a Sikh should live.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar's first line. Your line was the name is truth. Today, the two words that come next. Day eleven.

A boss with someone's job in their hands. A bully at the bus stop. And on the other side, a grudge kept for years. Fear and hate are strange twins: people fear those with power over them, resent those who wronged them, and between the two they can fill a whole life. In the root verse, Guru Nanak describes God with two words that cut right through both.
screen: `A BOSS, A BULLY.` → `A GRUDGE KEPT FOR YEARS.` → `TWO WORDS THAT CUT THROUGH BOTH.`

segments.voice: Nirbhau. Nirvair. Nir means without. Bhau means fear. Vair means enmity, the settled hostility of an enemy. So: without fear, without hate. Why together? Fear is what you feel toward something that could hurt you. Hate is what you feel toward something you think is against you. A God who is one, who holds everything, has nothing outside to fear and no enemy to hate. The verse goes on: beyond time, never born, existing by itself, known by the Guru's grace. But these two words have a life of their own, because Sikhs don't only say them about God. They take them as a picture of who a person can become. The ninth Guru, Guru Tegh Bahadur, wrote a short verse describing the wise person as one who frightens no one, and is frightened by no one. Both halves matter. Fearless isn't enough if it makes you frightening. Gentle isn't enough if it makes you afraid. So nirbhau, nirvair isn't only a description to admire from a distance. It's a direction.
screen: `NIR — WITHOUT.` · `BHAU, FEAR. VAIR, HATE.` · `FRIGHTENS NO ONE, FEARS NO ONE.` · `NOT JUST ABOUT GOD. A DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: Breathe, and name one thing you're afraid of. Then bring to mind one person you hold something against. Loosen your grip on both, only a little. If you like, let the words go out with the breath: nirbhau, nirvair.
The Mool Mantar, line two. Nirbhau, nirvair: without fear, without hate. Said of God, and taken as a direction for a life. Eleventh word.
Your line: nirbhau, nirvair. Less fear and less hate, both at once, which is harder than either alone. Day eleven.

12.title: honest work
12.hook: honest work; Nanak's three pillars start here
12.howItsDone: Sikhs are taught to live as householders and to earn their living honestly through their own work, and kirat karni is named with sharing and remembering the name as one of the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mool Mantar, line two: without fear, without hate. Today, the first of three pillars Sikhs build a life on. Day twelve.

A mountaintop. A begging bowl. A cave. The classic pictures of a holy man: someone who gave everything away, or left his family to meditate alone. Guru Nanak, back from his years on the road, chose differently. He spent the rest of his life on a farm by a river, plowing fields, raising a family, growing food. The founder of a faith, with his hands in the dirt.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINTOP. THE BEGGING BOWL.` → `NANAK CHOOSES A FARM.` → `THE FIRST OF THREE PILLARS.`

segments.voice: Kirat karni. Kirat means honest labor, the work of your hands and your head. Karni means to do. So: do honest work. Earn your living, and earn it cleanly. Sikhs often describe daily life as resting on three pillars, and this is the first. In Nanak's day, some seekers left ordinary life behind: work, family and home, living on alms. Nanak honored sincere seekers wherever he met them. But the life he taught was the householder's. You don't have to leave the world to find God; you find God in the middle of it, in the field, in the shop, at the kitchen table. So in his last years, at Kartarpur, the Guru farmed. A line in the scripture sums it up. In paraphrase: the one who eats what they've earned by their own effort, and gives some of it away with their own hand, recognizes the path. Notice the word honest. Work without cheating, without exploiting anyone, without taking what isn't yours. The first pillar isn't in a temple. It's on Monday morning.
screen: `KIRAT — HONEST LABOR. KARNI — TO DO.` · `NOT LEAVING THE WORLD. LIVING IN IT.` · `THE GURU WHO FARMED.` · `EARNED BY EFFORT, WITHOUT CHEATING.`

segments.voice: Look at your hands for a moment. Think about the work they do: paid work, housework, schoolwork, caring for someone. Pick one piece of it that's coming up, and picture doing it cleanly: no corner cut, nothing taken that isn't yours. Stay with that picture.
Kirat karni. Honest work: earning a living by your own effort, without cheating anyone. The first pillar. Twelfth word.
Your line: earn it clean. The shortcut nobody would notice is exactly where this pillar stands. Day twelve.

13.title: share what you earn
13.howItsDone: Sikhs practice vand chakna by sharing food, time and income with others; many give dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings, to the gurdwara, the langar or people in need.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kirat karni. Your line was earn it clean. Earning honestly is half of it. Today, the other half. Day thirteen.

A kid on the school bus has a bag of chips, and a friend is looking at it. There's a tiny moment where the kid decides: hold it tighter, or tip the bag over and say, want some? Most of us are still making that decision, just with bigger bags: a paycheck, a spare room, an afternoon. Today, the second pillar.
screen: `A BAG OF CHIPS ON THE BUS.` → `HOLD IT TIGHTER, OR TIP IT OVER?` → `THE SECOND PILLAR.`

segments.voice: Vand chakna. Vand means to share, to divide into portions. Chakna means to eat, to take your part. Share, and then eat. Notice the order. Not eat, and share what's left over. Share first, then enjoy what's yours. Yesterday's line from the scripture praised the one who earns by effort and gives some away with their own hand. Today is that second half. Your own hand: not a tax, not a charity you've never seen. Many Sikhs give in a particular way called dasvandh, a tenth: a tenth of what they earn, set aside for others and the community, the langar, the gurdwara, someone in need. Some give exactly a tenth, some give what they can, and some give their time instead. And the two pillars lean on each other. Honest work alone could make a hard worker who keeps everything. Sharing alone could be generous with money that wasn't fairly earned. Together: earn cleanly, then let some of it go. The langar from day two runs on exactly this.
screen: `VAND — SHARE. CHAKNA — EAT.` · `SHARE FIRST, THEN ENJOY.` · `DASVANDH — A TENTH.` · `EARN CLEAN, THEN LET SOME GO.`

segments.voice: Think about what came into your hands this week: money, food, time, a skill, a kindness. Pick one thing, and picture dividing it, the way you'd tip the bag over. Picture who you'd hand a portion to, and their face when you do. Stay with that.
Vand chakna. Share, then eat: dividing what you've earned so others have a portion too. The second pillar. Thirteenth word.
Your line: share it first. Not what's left over at the end, but the first portion. Day thirteen.

14.title: the third pillar
14.hook: the third pillar — remember the name, on the breath
14.carry: earn it clean, share it first, keep the name
14.howItsDone: Sikhs practice naam japna by repeating Waheguru in simran, often on the breath or with prayer beads, by reciting daily prayers and by singing the scripture together in kirtan; with honest work and sharing it forms the three pillars of Sikh life.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vand chakna. Your line was share it first. Today, the third pillar, the one that holds the other two up. Day fourteen.

A stool with two legs holds someone for a moment, if they're careful. Add a third leg, and it holds all day. Honest work, sharing what you earn: both solid. But a person could do both and still run on empty: busy, generous, and forgetting what any of it is for. In the Sikh telling, there's a third leg.
screen: `A STOOL WITH TWO LEGS.` → `BUSY, GENEROUS, AND EMPTY.` → `THE THIRD LEG.`

segments.voice: Naam japna. Naam, the name from day ten: not just a label, but the whole presence of God. Japna means to repeat, to keep saying. So: keep the name. Remember God, again and again, all through the day. Its everyday form has its own word: simran, remembrance. How do you remember something all day long? You tie it to something you do all day anyway. You breathe. Wahe on the in-breath, guru on the out-breath: the word from day one. Some Sikhs do it sitting still before dawn, some with prayer beads, some while they drive or cook. If you've ever wondered whether simply repeating Waheguru counts, it's one of the most common ways Sikhs practice. It can be silent, or a whole room singing the scripture to drums and harmonium. Here's why it sits beside work and sharing. Without it, honest work can turn into pride: look how hard I work. Sharing can turn into a show: look how much I give. Remembering keeps both humble, because it reminds you where the strength to work, and everything you share, came from. And remembering without working or sharing would float off into the clouds. Earn it clean, share it first, keep the name. Three legs.
screen: `NAAM — THE NAME. JAPNA — TO REPEAT.` · `SIMRAN — WAHE IN, GURU OUT.` · `IT KEEPS WORK AND GIVING HUMBLE.` · `WORK, SHARE, REMEMBER, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Feel what you're sitting on, and how it holds you up without your thinking about it. Breathe slowly. If you'd like, let the name ride on the breath: Wahe in, guru out. If that word isn't yours, let each breath carry one thing you want to remember is real. Keep coming back to it.

Naam japna. Keeping the name: remembering God through the day, often on the breath, as simran. The third pillar. Fourteenth word. Seva, Ik Onkar, the root verse twice, kirat karni, vand chakna, naam japna: that's week two.
Your line: earn it clean, share it first, keep the name. That's the whole stool. Next week: the company, the door, the spirit and the book. Day fourteen.
